d.title: Four knobs, and the two that move cost are not among them
d.caption: **`max_output_tokens` caps one reply, and the bill is dominated by input** — so tuning temperature and output caps while sending fifty turns of history and fourteen tool declarations is optimising the smaller half. The two settings that actually control spend live elsewhere: how much conversation you send (`include_contents`, compaction and caching) and how many declarations ride along on every call. **The temperature guidance is the one to internalise:** below about 0.3 for anything that calls tools, because tool-choice accuracy and instruction-following both degrade as it rises.

d.title: Two layers of resilience, and the quality drop neither of them reports
d.caption: **Retry first, fall back second** — per-request retry options handle the transient error inside one model, and `FallbackModel` handles the case where that model is simply unavailable. Both protect availability. **Neither protects the answer:** a fallback to a weaker model succeeds, returns something worse, and nothing in the invocation says so. That makes recording which model actually answered a requirement rather than a nicety, because otherwise a quota incident presents as a mysterious week of degraded quality.

d.title: Four ways to reach a model, and one contract underneath all of them
d.caption: **Everything in this table is a `BaseLlm` producing `LlmResponse` objects from an async generator, which is why the last row works at all.** The scripted model used throughout this course is not a testing special case — it is the same interface the real adapters implement, so an agent cannot tell the difference. That is what makes testing without a network straightforward rather than a mocking exercise. **The LiteLLM row is the one to reach for by default** for a non-Google provider: one line, maintained elsewhere, and it covers OpenAI, Azure, Bedrock and Ollama alike.

d.title: part.thought is the filter, and forgetting it shows the user the working-out
d.caption: **A client that renders every text part shows the agent talking to itself** — including, sometimes, the parts where it considered and rejected something, which is a worse disclosure than it first sounds. The flag is right there on the part, and filtering on it is the same discipline as filtering on `event.partial` when streaming. **Showing reasoning can be a deliberate product decision; showing it by accident is not one**, and the two are indistinguishable from the outside.

d.title: Two methods, and what a planner actually is
d.caption: **Strip the name away and `PlanReActPlanner` is a long instruction plus a function that splits the response on tags.** Seeing that clearly answers both halves of the decision: reach for a planner when you want the reasoning in a form your code can inspect and audit, and do not when you simply want better answers — a thinking-capable model with `BuiltInPlanner` gets you there without a parser to maintain. **A custom planner earns its place when your domain has a fixed procedure**: a triage sequence, a compliance checklist, an order of checks that must precede an action.

d.title: Model class or callback, and the subclass trick in between
d.caption: **Both can intercept a model call, and the question is what the interception depends on.** A callback sees the agent, the session and the state and applies per agent — right for anything that turns on *who is asking*, like a per-user cache or a guardrail. A model subclass sees only the request and applies everywhere that model is used — right for provider-level concerns: a shared cache, a gateway, instrumentation you want regardless of which agent made the call. **And the subclass trick is usually what people actually want:** extend the provider's own class, so you keep all of its behaviour and add yours in one method.
